## plugin:context7:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

lastPrompt: You orchestrator. Delegate to subagents!  Resolve issues #223 to #238. Ask your questions first, so that you can further work in autonomy

content.text: I'll pull the issues first, then come back with questions.

input.command:
for n in $(seq 223 238); do echo "=== #$n ==="; gh issue view $n --json number,title,state,labels,body 2>/dev/null | jq -r '"\(.state) | \(.title)
labels: \(.labels|map(.name)|join(", "))
---

The snippet-question leaves the instructions for the "snippet editor" in the scrollback. Unnecessary. ``` ? What is /opt/pcsw-uat-vendor on pc1? One application — /opt/pcsw-uat-vendor is what would be reproduced on pc2 ? How should pc2 get /opt/pcsw-uat-app? ◆ /opt/pcsw-uat-app install These commands run on pc2 with nobody watching — there is no keyboard attached to them, so a command that asks a question (e.g. a debconf prompt) hangs the sync instead of failing. Log only shows the "apt-get" commands (in DEBUG, as required), but nothing in FULL log. FULL log must list every item action install/remove/update/... of every package-sync job. If that is not in docs/planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md yet, add it and apply it to everything that flows from there, a.o. docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md, docs/dev/package-sync-scenario-coverage.md, tests, code, docs.

content.subject: #226 Drop "report" prefix from version-difference lines
content.description: Render as `tree: pc1 has X, pc2 has Y` — no leading word, no duplicated source version.

content.subject: #227 Per-case title and explanation-first for collateral question
content.description: Name the machine explicitly ("marked as pc2's own"), lift the concrete explanation above the key legend, and make the title case-specific if the question is raised per item.

content.subject: #228 Retitle repository-deletion question
content.description: "Delete apt repositories pc1 no longer has" instead of "Delete repositories pc1 no longer has (apt)".

content.subject: #229 Clearer snap version question
content.description: Title "Align snap package versions", key label "align", detail names the source of the revision.

content.description: Title asks "How should pc2 get X?" but the options are install/skip/never — retitle to the install decision.

content.subject: #231 --allow-first-sync is ignored
content.description: Flag set on the command line yet the first-sync overwrite confirmation still appears. Trace CLI -> context -> confirmation check and fix.

content.subject: #233 Narrow the snapd auto-refresh hold to snap_sync
content.description: Hold is taken before apt_sync runs, far wider than needed. Scope it to the snap sync window.

content.subject: #234 snapd pause logged twice
content.description: Determine whether the two DEBUG lines are source+target (correct) or a genuine double-pause, and fix or clarify accordingly.

content.subject: #235 flatpak_sync shows no progress line while applying
content.description: Status line sits in flatpak_sync with no progress line while changes apply. Report progress the way apt_sync/snap_sync do.

content.subject: #236 Snippet editor instructions should not stay in scrollback
content.description: Other questions collapse to title+answer after answering; the multiline snippet prompt leaves its instruction block behind.

content.description: Registry stores the body with trailing whitespace, forcing an ugly YAML block. Strip at capture, before anything is done with it.

content.description: Per-item install/remove/upgrade actions appear only in the DEBUG command trace. Add the requirement to package-sync-user-requirements.md and cascade it: conformance criteria, scenario coverage, tests, code, docs.

Two findings you should know about:

**#225 landed on the fallback, not live rendering.** It was tested under a real pty rather than reasoned about: with Live auto-refreshing, `Prompt.ask` writes onto the live region's last row and the next 10 Hz tick erases it — the question survived ~100 ms. Rich's `LiveRender` anchors at the cursor and rewrites upward, clobbering any output it didn't route itself; prompt_toolkit screens are worse. Fixing it properly means owning the input loop. So the last frame now stays in scrollback above the question, which is what your issue named as the acceptable fallback.

**#231 was narrower than the issue suggested.** `--allow-out-of-order` was never broken — `_check_out_of_order` already short-circuits before reaching the confirmer. Only `--allow-first-sync` reached the prompt. The confirmer fix covers both paths regardless.

#237 required amending `PKG-FR-SNIPPET-VERBATIM`, which said snippets are stored "exactly as written" — directly contradicted by stripping. That's now worded to permit the capture-time strip.

All 15 pushed; CI is running on PR #206. One correction to what I told you earlier about #238, and one thing to decide.

**#238's premise was wrong, and it matters.** Nothing was suppressing the `sl` line — it *was* in the FULL log, and apt is not batched (`packages.install` issues one `apt-get` per diff). The line read `install sl (6.03-1)`: no manager, no machine, and visually indistinguishable from the thousands of DEBUG `apt-get install …` traces surrounding it, which is why a grep found only the commands. It also had zero test coverage. The fix is therefore about identifiability, not about a missing write: the line is now `apt: install sl (6.03-1) on nomad`, emitted from `PackageSyncJob._converge_one` so all four managers share it. The requirement, `PKG-FR-LOG-ACTIONS`, conformance traceability (135→136 articles) and matrix rows J172/J173 all landed as you asked.

**#235's cause was the shared framework, not flatpak.** Progress was reported only *after* each item completed, and the UI creates a job's bar on the first update — so any single-item job showed no bar at all, for its entire duration. Reporting now happens before each item and carries the item name; flatpak additionally reports its pre-loop remote provisioning, which is the silent window your screenshot caught.

One housekeeping note: the two final agents shared the working tree, and `b04edaef` swept the J172/J173 matrix rows into its commit rather than `971ec936`. The content is all on the branch — only the attribution is off. Say the word if you want that untangled; I'd leave it.

Once CI is green I'll take the lock and drive a real `pc-switcher sync` on pc1 to eyeball the TUI changes — #223 wrapping, #225 context-during-prompt, #227's new screen layout, #236's collapse and #235's progress bar are all things only a real terminal can confirm. === PR body ===
Replicates installed packages from source to target across apt, snap and flatpak, plus the repository/keyring/remote state those installs depend on, with every difference surfaced for an explicit decision before any change is applied.

## What this delivers

- Three jobs — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync` — over a shared package-sync core (declarative manifest capture, item-level convergence via each ecosystem's own tooling; package databases are never rsynced, see ADR-020).
- A `PackagePhaseCoordinator` that runs every enabled manager's `plan()`, renders **one** batched review across all managers, then runs `apply()`. No manager can mutate the target before the others have diffed.
- Removals presented in their own group with a concrete removal verb, never sharing a group with installs, so a bulk tick cannot silently delete.
- The full diff-class taxonomy: missing-on-target, extra-on-target, version-mismatch, held/pinned, repo-unavailable, unreproducible. Versions float; a mismatch is reported with both versions and never force-downgraded.
- `/etc/apt` repository state as items — sources, per-repo keyrings, legacy trust keys, pins, apt config — converged in apt's required order, transactionally, with rollback if `apt-get update` fails.
- Machine-local decision files (skip-always), inert in both source and target roles, never synced.
- A shared, synced install-snippet registry for items no package manager can reproduce.
- Enabling a package job automatically excludes that ecosystem's store from `folder_sync`; package jobs run before `folder_sync` so apps are provisioned before their data lands.

## Process

Planned, then peer-reviewed by Codex (gpt-5.5) against the repo. That review found nine defects, all independently re-verified and fixed by replanning before any code was written — including that the original design would have let `apt_sync` mutate the target before the other managers had diffed, and that `send_file` (plain SFTP as the SSH user) could never have written into `/etc/apt`.

A deep code review after implementation found two further blockers, both fixed with regression tests: a `KeyError` crash path that violated continue-on-item-failure, and `install` without `-D` failing on targets where `/etc/apt/keyrings` does not exist.

All 15 issues are resolved, verified, and labelled `status:done`. Lock released, VMs back at baseline.

**Verification is complete on all three levels you asked for.** Local gate green (ruff, format, codespell, basedpyright, 4468 unit tests). PR #206 green on all nine checks including the 38-minute VM integration suite. And a real pc1→pc2 run at branch tip `971ec93` on a 100-column pty confirmed all 14 observable behaviours against saved captures — including an apply run that actually converged pc2 (`sl` installed and held, `cmatrix` absent, `fortunes`/`fortunes-min` removed via the collateral answer, `/opt/pcsw-uat-app` created from the snippet).

Three things to note:

**Two issues did not need the fix they asked for**, and I did not force one. #234 was never a double-pause — one call site looping source and target — so only the log's legibility changed. #233's narrowing would have reopened a real race, since `folder_sync` mirrors `~/snap/<app>/<rev>` by the revision `snap_sync` just converged; you chose to keep the wide window and fix the reporting, and the log line now states exactly that reasoning on the machine it applies to.

**#238's premise turned out to be wrong** — the line was already being written at FULL level and apt was never batched. What was actually missing was identifiability and any test coverage at all. Worth knowing, because the requirement I added (`PKG-FR-LOG-ACTIONS`) is now what stops it regressing.

**One new finding, outside the scope you gave me, so I left it alone**: `snap_sync.py:829,831` writes FULL log lines as `source snap refresh.hold: (none)` / `target snap refresh.hold: (none)`, using role words where the runbook's own rule requires hostnames. Say the word and I'll file it or fix it.

One loose end I'd leave as-is unless you disagree: commit `b04edaef` swept the J172/J173 coverage-matrix rows into its message instead of `971ec936`, because two agents shared the working tree. All the content is on the branch; only the attribution is off.

async def _hold_snap_autorefresh(self) -> None:
        """Pause snapd AUTOMATIC refreshes on both hosts for the sync window (decision 4).

        Gated on `sync_jobs.snap_sync` being enabled and skipped in dry-run (writing
        `refresh.hold` is a system mutation; ADR-014/D-12). Captures each host's prior
        `refresh.hold` first so `_cleanup` can restore it exactly, marks the hold engaged,
        then applies a timed hold on each host WHOSE PRIOR POLICY IT COULD READ. Only touches
        the system-wide `refresh.hold` option — never per-snap holds — and never blocks the
        manual `--revision` convergence snap_sync performs.

        A host whose capture failed is left untouched (`PKG-FR-SNAP-REFRESH-PAUSE`). The
        capture is what makes the write reversible: without a pre-sync value there is nothing
        to put back, so setting the option would replace an unknown policy — possibly the
        user's own indefinite hold — with a timed one that expires into "no hold at all". The
        cost is running unpaused on that host, which risks a mid-run auto-refresh; that trade
        is the criterion's, and it is the same one `_restore_snap_hold` makes on the way out.
        """
        if self._dry_run or not self._config.sync_jobs.get("snap_sync", False):
            return

        self._snap_hold_prior_source, self._snap_hold_readable_source = await self._capture_snap_hold(Host.SOURCE)
        self._snap_hold_prior_target, self._snap_hold_readable_target = await self._capture_snap_hold(Host.TARGET)
        # Engage BEFORE applying so a partially-applied hold is still restored in _cleanup.
        self._snap_hold_engaged = True
        for host, prior, readable in (
            (Host.SOURCE, self._snap_hold_prior_source, self._snap_hold_readable_source),
            (Host.TARGET, self._snap_hold_prior_target, self._snap_hold_readable_target),
        ):
            if not readable:
                self._logger.warning(
                    "Not pausing snapd auto-refresh on %s: its refresh.hold could not be read, so a hold "
                    "written here could not be put back. The sync continues unpaused on that machine.",
                    self._machine_name(host),
                    extra={"job": "orchestrator", "host": host.value},
                )
                continue
            # One line per machine, naming it (#234). The pause is two separate writes of
            # the SAME command text, one per host, so the DEBUG trace shows the identical
            # `snap set system refresh.hold` twice; a single "on both hosts" summary left a
            # reader grepping the log unable to tell that pair from one pause applied twice.
            # The line also states its owner and its span (#233): the pause happens before
            # the first job, which read as an unexplained stop with no component behind it.
            self._logger.info(
                "Pausing snapd auto-refresh on %s for the whole run — held by the orchestrator, not by "
                "snap_sync alone, because snap_sync converges each snap's revision and folder_sync then "
                "mirrors that revision's data directory; a refresh between the two drops it from the mirror",
                self._machine_name(host),
                extra={"job": "orchestrator", "host": host.value},
            )

# Python Development Conventions

Apply to Python code/projects. New or owner-controlled projects: use defaults. Existing: follow project config (Python version, deps, tests, lint, CI) unless explicitly migrating. Use modern standards for supported version.

## Python Version and Modern Practices

- New Python projects: target >=3.14
- Existing projects: use modern syntax for configured version
- Use modern type syntax: e.g. `str | None` instead of `Optional[str]`, `list[str]` instead of `List[str]`
- Include `from __future__ import annotations` when improves annotation behavior for Python version
- Use `@override` for method overrides when available in Python version
- Prefer `StrEnum` for string-based enums when available in Python version
- Prefer `Path` from pathlib for local filesystem paths

## Project Setup and Developer Workflows

- MUST use uv for running code, managing dependencies in new projects
- Existing projects: use project's workflow. Don't replace Poetry/Hatch/tox/Makefiles unless asked
- Use plain uv commands: `uv sync`, `uv run ...`, `uv add`, etc. Avoid `uv pip`. NEVER use `uv pip install` unless project intentionally uses uv's pip-compatible interface
- Use `codespell` for checking typos in code/comments
- Use `ruff` for linting, formatting
- Use `basedpyright` for type checking
- Use `pytest` for testing

## Code Quality Standards

- Full type annotations for function signatures, modern syntax per Python version
- Import types from correct modules (e.g., use `collections.abc` not `typing` for collection types)
- Proper error handling with specific exception types, meaningful messages
- Single responsibility principle, keep functions focused
- Use context managers for resource management
- Prefer composition over inheritance
- Self-documenting code with meaningful names
- Follow PEP 8 (max 119 chars), use Python strengths, avoid anti-patterns

## Documentation Philosophy

- Document architectural decisions, design patterns
- Concise docstrings: focus on "why" not obvious "what"
- Explain complex logic rationales inline when needed
- Use backticks for variable/parameter names in docstrings
- Avoid repetitive or obvious comments

## Testing Strategy

- Small focused tests, clear locality. Use repo's layout (colocated, `tests/` tree, doctests)
- Avoid trivial tests that test language itself
- Simple assertions over complex pytest fixtures when possible
- Test edge cases, errors, boundary values
- Mock external dependencies, I/O operations appropriately
- Mocked integration behavior: add real-dep integration coverage where practical
- Never use `assert False` - raise `AssertionError` with explanation instead

## Performance Optimization Techniques

- Use appropriate data structures (sets for membership, deque for queues, etc.)
- Implement generators for memory-efficient iteration over large datasets
- Apply caching strategies where beneficial
- Utilize built-in functions/libraries (itertools, collections, functools)
- Consider algorithmic complexity, choose efficient algorithms
- Profile code using cProfile, line_profiler, or memory_profiler before optimizing

## Error Handling and Type Checking

- Use `# pyright: ignore` sparingly, always with explanation
- Raise `AssertionError` with descriptive messages for invariant violations
- Handle exceptions at appropriate levels, avoid bare except
- Use specific exception types that convey meaning

## File Operations Best Practices

- Prefer `Path` objects for local filesystem paths
- Atomic file writing for user data, config, state or other where partial output harmful
- Use context managers for file operations
- Handle encoding explicitly (default UTF-8)

## Core Principles

- Pragmatic: avoid over-engineering, premature optimization
- Leverage stdlib first. Use third-party packages sparingly
- Code clarity over clever tricks
- Aim for functional, clean, maintainable, performant code

# Python Development Commands

New or owner-controlled projects → uv. Existing repos → follow project's setup unless asked.

## Package Management with uv

Prefer uv (new projects). Skip `uv pip` unless project uses it. Don't replace other package managers without ask.

```bash
# Initialize new project
uv init

# Add dependencies
uv add package_name
uv add --dev ipykernel pytest ruff basedpyright  # dev dependencies

# Sync dependencies
uv sync

# Show installed packages
uv tree
uv tree --package package_name

# Run commands in virtual environment
uv run python script.py
uv run pytest
```

## Testing with pytest

```bash
# Run all tests
uv run pytest

# Run tests with coverage
uv run pytest --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing

# Run specific test file or function
uv run pytest tests/test_module.py
uv run pytest tests/test_module.py::test_function

# Run tests matching pattern
uv run pytest -k "pattern"

# Run tests with verbose output
uv run pytest -v

# Run tests and stop on first failure
uv run pytest -x
```

## Linting and Formatting with ruff

```bash
# Format code
uv run ruff format .

# Check linting issues
uv run ruff check .

# Fix auto-fixable issues
uv run ruff check --fix .

# Check specific file
uv run ruff check path/to/file.py
```

## Type Checking with basedpyright

```bash
# Type check entire project
uv run basedpyright

# Type check specific file
uv run basedpyright path/to/file.py
```

## Code Quality Checks

```bash
# Run all quality checks (typical CI pipeline)
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ruff check .
uv run basedpyright
uv run pytest

# Check for common typos
uv run codespell
```

## Profiling and Performance

```bash
# Profile with cProfile
uv run python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py

# Profile with line_profiler
uv run kernprof -l -v script.py

# Memory profiling
uv run python -m memory_profiler script.py
```

## Common Development Patterns

```bash
# Check outdated packages
uv tree --outdated

# Clean pyc files and caches only when explicitly requested
find . -type d -name "__pycache__" -exec rm -rf {} +
find . -type d -name ".pytest_cache" -exec rm -rf {} +
find . -type d -name ".ruff_cache" -exec rm -rf {} +
find . -type f -name "*.pyc" -delete
```

name: log-message-never-repeats-the-host
description: Every pc-switcher log line already carries its host; naming the machine inside the message text is duplication
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Every pc-switcher log record carries the host it happened on (`extra={"host": ...}`, rendered on each line). Do not name the machine inside the message text as well.

**Why:** the host is structural metadata on the line, not part of the sentence. Repeating it makes the message longer without telling the reader anything the line doesn't already show, and it invites splitting one announcement into one-per-host purely to have somewhere to put the name.

**How to apply:** when a message would read "... on pc2", drop that clause and let the line's host carry it. Applies to an action affecting both machines too — announce it once rather than once per host. The exception is text naming a machine that is *not* the line's own host (e.g. "pc1 has X, pc2 has Y" in a comparison, or a remediation command the user runs elsewhere). See [[executor-mutates-marker]] for the other half of what a write must record.

content.content:
9-happen: the literal shell command as it will be passed to the shell, or the local path and
10-remote destination of a file transfer. Nothing is paraphrased or reconstructed for display,
11-because a display string that differs from what runs is worse than no display at all.
12-
13-Distinct from `pcswitcher.confirmer.Confirmer`, which gates ONE coarse decision per run
14-(first-sync overwrite, out-of-order topology) and falls back to an `--allow-*` flag when
15:nobody is there to answer. This gate has no such fallback and never auto-proceeds: it is
16-opt-in per run and refused outright without a TTY (`cli.sync`), because a gate that
17:auto-proceeds when unanswerable is precisely the failure it exists to prevent.
18-
19:Two outcomes only, with no default (the user must type one): proceed, or abort the whole
20-sync. There is deliberately no "skip this command" — a single reviewed item can span
21-several commands (apt source stage-then-promote, snap install-then-switch-channel), so
22-skipping one of them leaves that item half-applied, which is a worse state than either
23-finishing it or stopping.
24-
25-Generic on purpose, and invoked from exactly one place: `pcswitcher.executor`. Any caller
26-— job, orchestrator, helper — gates a write by passing `mutates="..."` to the executor
27-method it already uses, so there is no second API to remember and no per-job wiring. The
28-executor supplies `job` (from its `active_job` context variable) and `host` (from which
29-executor it is). Every write passes `mutates` except `folder_sync`'s rsync pass (#209);
--

62-            description: Short human phrase for what this achieves ("install firefox").

64-                a `send_file <local> -> <remote>` rendering for a transfer.

67:            None when the user chose to proceed.

70-            SyncAbortedByUser: The user typed "abort".

`SyncAborted` for the same reason an unparsable snippet registry raises it
        (`PKG-FR-REGISTRY-CONSENT`): the run must end for the user to repair something by
        hand, which is not this job failing and not the tool breaking.
        """
        stray: list[tuple[str, frozenset[str]]] = []
        if source_hold_names:
            stray.append((self.machines.source, source_hold_names - await self._probe.capture_source_installed()))
        if target_hold_names:
            stray.append((self.machines.target, target_hold_names - await self._installed_on_target()))
        for machine, names in stray:
            if not names:
                continue
            listed = ", ".join(sorted(names))
            raise SyncAborted(
                f"{machine} holds apt package(s) it does not have installed: {listed}. "
                f"A hold on a package the machine lacks freezes nothing and refuses every later attempt to "
                f"install it. Clear it on {machine} with `sudo apt-mark unhold {listed}`, then sync again."
            )

    @staticmethod
    def _marked_packages(decisions: Mapping[str, DecisionEntry]) -> frozenset[str]:
        """The package NAMES one machine's decision file records machine-specific.

        Two callers need the same fact about different files: the collateral question reads
        the target's (`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MARKED`), and the hold diff reads each machine's own
        so a mark on a package makes its hold inert too (`diff_apt_holds`).
        """
        return frozenset(package_name(item_id) for item_id in decisions if item_id.startswith(APT_PACKAGE_ID_PREFIX))

    def _target_marked_packages(self) -> frozenset[str]:
        """Package names the TARGET recorded machine-specific, from the decision file
        `_plan_packages` has just read (`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MARKED`).

        These never reach a review of their own — `filter_inert` drops them from the target
        manifest before anything is diffed — so the collateral question is the only place
        the user can be told a mark is about to be overrun.
        """
        _source_decisions, target_decisions = self._plan_decisions
        return self._marked_packages(target_decisions)

"""Per-action confirmation gate behind `--confirm-each-command`.

Generic infrastructure, not one job family's: it lives beside `executor.py`, which is its
only caller, and gates every write any job makes. A package sync is simply where the need
is sharpest — such a run converges dozens of small mutating commands — `apt-get install`,
`snap remove`, `sudo install` into `/etc/apt`, an SFTP push of the snippet registry — each
of which was approved only in aggregate, as a ticked line in a batched review. This gate
inserts one prompt before every single one of them, showing the EXACT operation about to
happen: the literal shell command as it will be passed to the shell, or the local path and
remote destination of a file transfer. Nothing is paraphrased or reconstructed for display,
because a display string that differs from what runs is worse than no display at all.

Distinct from `pcswitcher.confirmer.Confirmer`, which gates ONE coarse decision per run
(first-sync overwrite, out-of-order topology) and falls back to an `--allow-*` flag when
nobody is there to answer. This gate has no such fallback and never auto-proceeds: it is
opt-in per run and refused outright without a TTY (`cli.sync`), because a gate that
auto-proceeds when unanswerable is precisely the failure it exists to prevent.

Two outcomes only, with no default (the user must type one): proceed, or abort the whole
sync. There is deliberately no "skip this command" — a single reviewed item can span
several commands (apt source stage-then-promote, snap install-then-switch-channel), so
skipping one of them leaves that item half-applied, which is a worse state than either
finishing it or stopping.

Generic on purpose, and invoked from exactly one place: `pcswitcher.executor`. Any caller
— job, orchestrator, helper — gates a write by passing `mutates="..."` to the executor
method it already uses, so there is no second API to remember and no per-job wiring. The
executor supplies `job` (from its `active_job` context variable) and `host` (from which
executor it is). Every write passes `mutates` except `folder_sync`'s rsync pass (#209);
`tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py` holds that line.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

from rich.console import Console
from rich.panel import Panel
from rich.prompt import Prompt
from rich.text import Text

from pcswitcher.confirmer import PausableUI
from pcswitcher.models import Host, SyncAborted, SyncAbortedByUser

__all__ = ["StepGate", "TerminalUIStepGate"]

_PROCEED = "p"
_ABORT = "a"


@runtime_checkable
class StepGate(Protocol):
    """A per-action confirmation gate: show one pending modification, block, decide."""

    async def confirm_action(self, *, job: str, host: Host, description: str, command: str) -> None:
        """Show a pending modification and block until the user decides.

        Args:
            job: Name of the job about to modify something (panel heading, log context).
            host: Which machine the modification lands on.
            description: Short human phrase for what this achieves ("install firefox").
            command: The operation VERBATIM — the shell command as it will be executed, or
                a `send_file <local> -> <remote>` rendering for a transfer.

        Returns:
            None when the user chose to proceed.

        Raises:
            SyncAbortedByUser: The user typed "abort".
            SyncAborted: The prompt could not be answered (EOF / Ctrl-C), so nobody
                decided anything. Never swallowed into a silent "proceed".
        """
        ...


class TerminalUIStepGate:
    """`StepGate` backed by the Rich console and the live `TerminalUI`.

    Pauses the live display around the blocking prompt for the same reason
    `TerminalUIConfirmer` does — a Rich `Live` and a `Prompt.ask` cannot share the
    terminal — and resumes it in a `finally` so the display is handed back even when the
    prompt raises.

    Both machine names are required, not defaulted (`PKG-FR-NAME-THE-MACHINES`): this
    prompt is a question the user answers, so the machine about to be changed is named
    here by hostname, once, in the heading. That is why a `mutates=` phrase does not have
    to repeat it — the phrase says what the change does, the heading says where.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        console: Console,
        ui: PausableUI,
        *,
        source_hostname: str,
        target_hostname: str,
        logger: logging.Logger | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        self._console = console
        self._ui = ui
        self._hostnames = {Host.SOURCE: source_hostname, Host.TARGET: target_hostname}
        self._logger = logger if logger is not None else logging.getLogger("pcswitcher.step_gate")

    async def confirm_action(self, *, job: str, host: Host, description: str, command: str) -> None:
        extra = {"job": job, "host": host.value}
        hostname = self._hostnames[host]

        # Body is assembled as a `Text`, never a markup string: `command` is arbitrary
        # content (package names, file paths, snippet bodies) and a stray `[` in it would
        # otherwise be parsed as Rich markup and raise mid-prompt.
        body = Text()
        body.append(f"{job} → {hostname}\n", style="bold")
        body.append(f"{description}\n\n", style="dim")
        body.append(command, style="bold")

        self._ui.pause()
        try:
            self._console.print()
            self._console.print(Panel(body, title="Confirm modification", border_style="yellow"))
            self._console.print()
            # No `default=`: the user must type a choice. An accidental Enter re-prompts
            # rather than picking either outcome for them.
            response = Prompt.ask(
                f"[bold]Run this?[/bold] [{_PROCEED}] proceed  [{_ABORT}] abort sync",
                choices=[_PROCEED, _ABORT],
                show_choices=False,
            )
        except (EOFError, KeyboardInterrupt) as exc:
            # Unanswerable is not approval: the same rule the review applies to Ctrl-C.
            # Plain `SyncAborted` — an EOF means nobody was there to answer at all, so
            # this end of the run is not one to put on the user (#224).
            self._logger.warning("Confirmation prompt interrupted; aborting sync", extra=extra)
            raise SyncAborted(f"{job}: confirmation prompt interrupted before {description}") from exc
        finally:
            self._ui.resume()

        if response == _ABORT:
            self._logger.warning("Aborted by user at: %s", description, extra=extra)
            raise SyncAbortedByUser(f"{job}: aborted by user before {description} on {hostname}")
        self._logger.debug("Confirmed: %s", description, extra=extra)

async def start_persistent_remote_lock(
    executor: RemoteExecutor,
    source_hostname: str,
    session_id: str,
) -> RemoteProcess | None:
    """Start a persistent lock on remote machine via SSH.

    Uses the same lock file as the local source lock, ensuring a machine
    can only participate in one sync at a time (as source or target).

    Starts a long-running background process that holds the flock for the
    entire sync session. The lock is released when the process is terminated
    (via release_remote_lock()) or when the SSH connection closes.

    Args:
        executor: Remote executor for running commands on target
        source_hostname: Hostname of source machine (for diagnostics)
        session_id: Session ID (for diagnostics)

    Returns:
        RemoteProcess object holding the lock, or None if lock is already held
    """
    lock_path = f"$HOME/.local/share/pc-switcher/{LOCK_FILE_NAME}"
    holder_info = f"target:{source_hostname}:{session_id}"

    # First create directory and write holder info to lock file
    # Note: Use $HOME instead of ~ because ~ doesn't expand inside double quotes
    setup_result = await executor.run_command(
        f'mkdir --parents "$HOME/.local/share/pc-switcher" && echo "{holder_info}" > "{lock_path}"',
        mutates="claim the sync lock file, overwriting any previous holder record",
    )
    if not setup_result.success:
        return None

    # Start persistent process that holds the lock.
    # flock --nonblock = non-blocking attempt; if the lock is already held it exits
    # immediately (non-zero). -c "read" otherwise blocks forever on stdin (which
    # never receives input), keeping the process — and the lock — alive until
    # terminated.
    cmd = f'flock --nonblock "{lock_path}" --command "read"'

    try:
        process = await executor.start_process(cmd)
        # Give flock time to either acquire the lock (and block on read) or
        # fail-fast. A process that has already exited means flock could NOT
        # acquire the lock — the target is already involved in another sync.
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
        if process.poll() is not None:
            await process.wait()  # reap the exited process
            return None
        return process
    except Exception:
        return None


async def release_remote_lock(process: RemoteProcess) -> None:
    """Release the persistent remote lock.

    Terminates the lock-holding process, which releases the flock.

    Args:
        process: RemoteProcess object returned by start_persistent_remote_lock()
    """
    await process.terminate()

async def _acquire_target_lock(self) -> None:
        """Acquire exclusive lock on target machine via SSH.

        Uses the same unified lock file as the source, ensuring the target
        machine cannot participate in any other sync while this one runs.
        """
        assert self._remote_executor is not None

        self._target_lock_process = await start_persistent_remote_lock(
            self._remote_executor, self._source_hostname, self._session_id
        )
        if self._target_lock_process is None:
            raise SyncLockedError(
                f"{self._target_hostname} is already involved in a sync.\n"
                f"{_stuck_lock_hint(self._target_hostname, '~/.local/share/pc-switcher/pc-switcher.lock')}"
            )

    async def _install_on_target_job(self) -> None:
        """Execute InstallOnTargetJob to ensure pc-switcher is on target.

        Runs AFTER pre-sync snapshots for rollback safety if installation fails.
        """
        context = self._create_job_context({})
        install_job = InstallOnTargetJob(context)

        # Validate first (though it just returns empty list)
        errors = await install_job.validate()
        if errors:
            error_msgs = [f"  - {e.host.value}: {e.message}" for e in errors]

def __init__(self, lock_path: Path) -> None:
        """Initialize lock with path.

        Args:
            lock_path: Path to lock file (e.g., ~/.local/share/pc-switcher/pc-switcher.lock)
        """
        self._lock_path = lock_path
        self._lock_fd: int | None = None

    def acquire(self, holder_info: str | None = None) -> bool:
        """Acquire exclusive lock non-blocking.

        Args:
            holder_info: Info to write to lock file for diagnostics (e.g., "source:hostname:session_id")

        Returns:
            True if lock acquired, False if already held by another process
        """
        self._lock_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        self._lock_fd = os.open(self._lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_RDWR)
        try:
            fcntl.flock(self._lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
            # Write holder info for diagnostics
            info = holder_info or str(os.getpid())
            os.ftruncate(self._lock_fd, 0)
            os.write(self._lock_fd, info.encode())
            return True
        except BlockingIOError:
            # Lock is held by another process
            os.close(self._lock_fd)
            self._lock_fd = None
            return False

    def get_holder_info(self) -> str | None:
        """Read info about process holding the lock.

        Returns:
            Holder info string or None if lock file doesn't exist or is empty
        """
        try:
            content = self._lock_path.read_text().strip()
            return content or None
        except FileNotFoundError:
            return None

    def release(self) -> None:
        """Release the lock.

        Safe to call multiple times. Does nothing if lock not held.
        Note: Lock is automatically released when process exits.
        """
        if self._lock_fd is not None:
            fcntl.flock(self._lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
            os.close(self._lock_fd)
            self._lock_fd = None

Both answers are in the code; here's what I verified.

**Why the lock is taken in a dry-run**

The lock is mutual exclusion, not a sync operation: source and target share one lock file so a machine can only be in one sync at a time (`lock.py:118-119`, `orchestrator.py:680-681`). It's acquired at SyncStep 3 (`orchestrator.py:502`) with **no dry-run guard** — compare the snapd hold at `orchestrator.py:1523`, which explicitly returns early when `self._dry_run`.

That's defensible for the *lock* itself: a dry-run reads the target's entire package and file state to compute the preview, and a concurrent real sync would shift that state underneath it. But that rationale is my inference — it isn't written down anywhere I could find.

**What is not defensible is the write.** `dry_run` is threaded into `JobContext` for jobs to honour; it is never consulted by `executor.py` or `lock.py`. So the command in your screenshot genuinely executes against pc2 — `--dry-run` writes the holder record to the target's lock file, contradicting its own docstring ("preview sync without making changes", `orchestrator.py:289`). Note the flock is what actually enforces exclusion; the `echo` is only diagnostics, so exclusion would survive without the write.

**Why there's no confirm for the release**

Because there is no write to confirm. `release_remote_lock` is `process.terminate()` (`lock.py:174`) — it kills the remote flock-holding process over the existing SSH channel. No `run_command`, no `send_file`, so no `mutates=` and nothing for the gate to show. The gate isn't missing anything here.

There's a related asymmetry worth knowing: **nothing ever clears the holder record.** Release drops the flock only, so pc2's lock file keeps `target:pc1:0d9461ef` after the sync ends — and the local source lock behaves the same (`lock.py:99-108` unlocks and closes, never truncates). Stale holder strings in those files are normal, not evidence of a stuck lock.

For completeness, the flock acquisition itself (`start_process` at `lock.py:153`) is deliberately ungated and is recorded as such in `tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py:218-220`: it takes an advisory lock on a file already written above it and changes no content.

Want me to file the dry-run write as a bug? The narrow fix is to skip the holder `echo` under `--dry-run` and let `flock` create the file, keeping exclusion while writing nothing.

content.text:
Confirmed. `Executor._announce` (`executor.py:174`) returns early when `mutates is None`, so the gate never sees it — and `start_process` *does* accept `mutates` (`executor.py:367`), it just isn't passed at `lock.py:153`.

So the split is:

| Command | `mutates=` | Gated |
|---|---|---|
| `mkdir --parents … && echo "target:pc1:…" > …lock` | yes (`lock.py:140`) | **yes** |
| `flock --nonblock …lock --command "read"` | no (`lock.py:153`) | **no** |

The justification is recorded in `tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py:218-220`: the flock "takes an advisory lock on a file already written above it; the process holds it and changes no content." That's literally true — an advisory lock changes no file content — but it reads the `mutates` contract as being about *content*, when what the gate exists to surface is a change to the machine. The flock is what actually seizes exclusive control of pc2 and makes every other sync fail; the `echo` is a diagnostic string nothing depends on. You're being asked to approve the cosmetic half and not the consequential half.

**One mitigation, and it's positional rather than designed.** The `echo` runs first, and `start_persistent_remote_lock` returns early if it fails (`lock.py:142-143`). Aborting at that prompt raises out of `run_command` before `start_process` is ever reached, so in practice today the flock never happens without your approval.

**Which means I have to walk back the fix I proposed.** I suggested skipping the `echo` under `--dry-run` and letting `flock` create the file. That would delete the only thing currently gating lock acquisition, so a dry-run would silently take an exclusive lock on pc2 with no prompt at all — strictly worse. Scratch that.

The honest options are: pass `mutates=` on the `start_process` call so the flock is gated on its own merits (and re-classify that audit entry), and separately decide whether `--dry-run` should be claiming the target lock at all. Those are two different questions and I'd file them as two issues rather than one. Want me to?

In pc-switcher, every command/transfer/process reaching either machine goes through `Executor` (`src/pcswitcher/executor.py`), which is also where the verbatim `DEBUG` trace (#210) and the `--confirm-each-command` confirmation gate live. A call that CHANGES a machine MUST pass `mutates="<short phrase>"`; reads must NOT.

```python
await self.target.run_command(cmd, login_shell=False)                              # read
await self.target.run_command(cmd, login_shell=False, mutates="install firefox")   # write
await self.target.send_file(local, remote, mutates="push the snippet registry")
await self.target.start_process(cmd, mutates="mirror /home with rsync")
```

Covers `run_command`, `start_process`, `send_file`, `get_file` — on the SOURCE executor as well as the target. For a modification that is neither a command nor a transfer (in-process file rewrite, e.g. `sync_history.record_role`), use `await executor.declare_modification(f"write {path} ...", mutates="...")` so it still passes the one funnel.

**Why:** the marker is opt-in, so a write that omits it is a change the user is never shown and never asked to confirm — it silently defeats the gate and leaves a hole in the debug trace. Gating reads would be equally wrong: it makes the prompts worthless to read. This is the single invariant the whole design rests on, and nothing detects a violation automatically yet.

**How to apply:** when adding or reviewing ANY code that writes to source or target, check the executor call carries `mutates=`. Never route a write around the executor with `subprocess`/`pathlib`/`sqlite3` directly — `declare_modification` is the escape hatch for genuinely in-process writes. Job classes have no mutation helpers of their own: they call the executors, and the gate is consulted inside `executor.py`, never per job. See [[pcswitcher-confirm-each-command]].

A package sync is simply where the need 5 is sharpest — such a run converges dozens of small mutating commands — `apt-get install`, 6 `snap remove`, `sudo install` into `/etc/apt`, an SFTP push of the snippet registry — each 7 of which was approved only in aggregate, as a ticked line in a batched review. This gate 8 inserts one prompt before every single one of them, showing the EXACT operation about to 9 happen: the literal shell command as it will be passed to the shell, or the local path and 10 remote destination of a file transfer. Nothing is paraphrased or reconstructed for display, 11 because a display string that differs from what runs is worse than no display at all. 12 13 Distinct from `pcswitcher.confirmer.Confirmer`, which gates ONE coarse decision per run 14 (first-sync overwrite, out-of-order topology) and falls back to an `--allow-*` flag when 15 nobody is there to answer. This gate has no such fallback and never auto-proceeds: it is 16 opt-in per run and refused outright without a TTY (`cli.sync`), because a gate that 17 auto-proceeds when unanswerable is precisely the failure it exists to prevent. 18 19 Two outcomes only, with no default (the user must type one): proceed, or abort the whole 20 sync. There is deliberately no "skip this command" — a single reviewed item can span 21 several commands (apt source stage-then-promote, snap install-then-switch-channel), so 22 skipping one of them leaves that item half-applied, which is a worse state than either 23 finishing it or stopping. 24 25 What is gated is everything that is not purely read-only, which is wider than "changes a 26 file": a `flock` that seizes the target's sync lock, a background process started and left 27 running, a `sudo` probe that primes the credential cache — each changes the machine while 28 writing nothing, and each is something a user stepping through a run must be able to 29 refuse. A call is ungated only when it can change no state at all. 30 31 Generic on purpose, and invoked from exactly one place: `pcswitcher.executor`. Any caller 32 — job, orchestrator, helper — reaches this gate by passing `mutates="..."` to the executor 33 method it already uses, so there is no second API to remember and no per-job wiring. 51	Everything reaching source/target goes through `Executor` (`executor.py`), which drives `--confirm-each-command` and the verbatim DEBUG trace. `run_command`/`start_process`/`send_file`/`get_file` MUST pass `mutates="<phrase>"` unless the call is PURELY read-only — it may be omitted only when the call can change no state at all: no file content, no process state, no lock or advisory state, no package-manager database, no credential cache. "Changes no file content" is NOT sufficient grounds to leave a call ungated. In-process changes (no shell command): `executor.declare_modification(...)`. Omitting it ships a change the user is never shown; `tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py` enforces this.

name: log-message-never-repeats-the-host
description: Every pc-switcher log line already carries its host; naming the machine inside the message text is duplication
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: a6fdf859-1f12-4daf-94eb-8369ba71837c
  modified: 2026-08-02T19:23:20.098Z
---

Every pc-switcher log record carries the host it happened on (`extra={"host": ...}`, rendered on each line). Do not name the machine inside the message text as well.

**Why:** the host is structural metadata on the line, not part of the sentence. Repeating it makes the message longer without telling the reader anything the line doesn't already show, and it invites splitting one announcement into one-per-host purely to have somewhere to put the name.

**How to apply:** when a message would read "... on pc2", drop that clause and let the line's host carry it. Applies to an action affecting both machines too — announce it once rather than once per host. The exception is text naming a machine that is *not* the line's own host (e.g. "pc1 has X, pc2 has Y" in a comparison, or a remediation command the user runs elsewhere). See [[executor-mutates-marker]] for the other half of what a write must record.

name: repr-mangles-shell-scripts
description: "f\"bash -c {script!r}\" silently turns a multi-line shell script into one broken line; use shlex.quote"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 6fd79944-5079-446f-99f7-bbe44c27ff4e
  modified: 2026-07-27T17:28:12.925Z
---

Passing a multi-line shell script to a shell via `f"sudo bash -c {SCRIPT!r}"` is broken: Python's `repr` renders each newline as the two characters `\` and `n`, so bash receives one line, dies on the first `{`, and the error is usually swallowed by a surrounding `|| true`. Use `shlex.quote(SCRIPT)`, which preserves real newlines.

**Why:** it fails silently and forever. `delete_all_snapshots` (`btrfs_snapshots.py`) shipped this way on 2026-01-01 and deleted nothing until 2026-07-27 — no caller checked its `CommandResult`, so the only symptom was snapshots and empty session folders accumulating on the test VMs, which was misread as a performance problem (#216) rather than a broken sweep. It surfaced only when a retention test started ranking its own sessions behind ~30 leftovers.

**How to apply:** when a shell command string is built in Python, read the DEBUG command trace — a literal `\n` in the logged command is the tell. Any executor helper whose result nobody checks needs a unit test that splits the command with `shlex.split` and asserts the script comes back with its newlines intact; a `bash -n` syntax check on the result costs nothing and needs no target machine. Related: [[executor-mutates-marker]].

---
name: pcswitcher-confirm-each-command
description: "pc-switcher --confirm-each-command gates every individual modification at the Executor level; two outcomes only (proceed / abort run), no skip, TTY required"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 45bab55c-d9a8-487c-8bb3-fb879deaa844
  modified: 2026-07-25T13:48:57.626Z
---

`pc-switcher sync <target> --confirm-each-command` shows every individual modification verbatim — the literal shell command, or `send_file <local> -> <remote>` — and requires an explicit **p** (proceed) or **a** (abort the whole sync). No default; Enter re-prompts. EOF/Ctrl-C is an abort, never approval. Refused at startup without a TTY on both stdin and stdout.

Design decisions and their reasons:

- **Gate lives in `executor.py`, not in `Job`.** An earlier draft put `run_mutating()`/`send_file_mutating()` helpers on the job base class; rejected because it made reads and writes asymmetric (different object, different call shape), forced a `login_shell`-ignored-for-source hack, and needed separate `gate=` plumbing for `DecisionFile`/`SnippetRegistry`. See [[executor-mutates-marker]].
- **No "skip this command".** One reviewed item can span several commands (apt source stage-then-promote, snap install-then-switch-channel), so skipping one leaves the item half-applied.
- **No non-interactive fallback**, unlike `Confirmer`'s `--allow-*` flags: a gate that auto-proceeds when unanswerable is the exact failure it exists to prevent.
- **Job label via `active_job` ContextVar**, not an executor attribute — executors are shared by all jobs, so a mutable attribute would be clobbered under future parallel execution; asyncio copies context per task. A parallel job loop must set the label per job TASK.
- **apt repository-group rollback stays N commands, not one `;`-joined command**, so a failing restore can be named by file; when any step fails the backup dir is KEPT (it holds the only copy of the pre-run content) and the failure text reads `ROLLBACK INCOMPLETE`.
- **snapd hold restore is gated too**, and `_restore_snap_hold` re-raises `SyncAbortedByUser` ahead of its broad `except Exception`; `_cleanup` catches it around that one call and still releases locks/connection — a prompt must never leak a lock.

**Why:** the batched package review approves *items*, not commands; one ticked line can expand into a simulation, an install, a hold, or a backup/stage/promote/update sequence. This flag is for auditing or debugging a run that is not yet trusted, not for everyday syncs.

**How to apply:** treat the flag as audit/debug tooling — correctness and completeness of coverage matter more than prompt ergonomics. When adding a write anywhere, the flag must cover it automatically, which is what [[executor-mutates-marker]] guarantees.

metadata:

`pc-switcher sync <target> --confirm-each-command` shows every individual modification verbatim — the literal shell command, or `send_file <local> -> <remote>` — and requires an explicit **p** (proceed) or **a** (abort the whole sync). No default; Enter re-prompts. EOF/Ctrl-C is an abort, never approval. Refused at startup without a TTY on both stdin and stdout.

Design decisions and their reasons:

- **Gate lives in `executor.py`, not in `Job`.** An earlier draft put `run_mutating()`/`send_file_mutating()` helpers on the job base class; rejected because it made reads and writes asymmetric (different object, different call shape), forced a `login_shell`-ignored-for-source hack, and needed separate `gate=` plumbing for `DecisionFile`/`SnippetRegistry`.
- **No "skip this command".** One reviewed item can span several commands (apt source stage-then-promote, snap install-then-switch-channel), so skipping one leaves the item half-applied.
- **No non-interactive fallback**, unlike `Confirmer`'s `--allow-*` flags: a gate that auto-proceeds when unanswerable is the exact failure it exists to prevent.
- **Job label via `active_job` ContextVar**, not an executor attribute — executors are shared by all jobs, so a mutable attribute would be clobbered under future parallel execution; asyncio copies context per task. A parallel job loop must set the label per job TASK.
- **apt repository-group rollback stays N commands, not one `;`-joined command**, so a failing restore can be named by file; when any step fails the backup dir is KEPT (it holds the only copy of the pre-run content) and the failure text reads `ROLLBACK INCOMPLETE`.
- **snapd hold restore is gated too**, and `_restore_snap_hold` re-raises `SyncAbortedByUser` ahead of its broad `except Exception`; `_cleanup` catches it around that one call and still releases locks/connection — a prompt must never leak a lock.

**Why:** the batched package review approves *items*, not commands; one ticked line can expand into a simulation, an install, a hold, or a backup/stage/promote/update sequence. This flag is for auditing or debugging a run that is not yet trusted, not for everyday syncs.

**How to apply:** treat the flag as audit/debug tooling — correctness and completeness of coverage matter more than prompt ergonomics. When adding a write anywhere, the flag must cover it automatically, which is what the `mutates=` rule in the repo's own CLAUDE.md guarantees.

The general lesson I'll apply going forward: a memory earns its place only if the fact has no home in the repo. Design rationale belongs in the code comment or the ADR next to the thing it explains — which is also where someone reading that code will actually find it.
